analysis.one_liner: Lets a new union get binding arbitration if first contract talks stall.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the House committee after 0 cosponsors signed on and no action in two years.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to form a union, the employer and the union have to negotiate a first contract. Under current law, an employer can simply refuse to agree to anything, and the union gets no contract. This bill would have set a timer: after 60 days without agreement, a mediator steps in, and after another 30 days, either side could send the remaining disputes to binding arbitration, meaning an independent arbitrator would decide the disputed terms and both sides would be bound by that decision.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly unionized workplaces gain the most. Today, a newly certified union can spend years trying to negotiate a first contract while the employer stalls, and many first contract efforts fail entirely, leaving workers with the union they voted for but no actual agreement on pay, scheduling, or benefits. A binding arbitration deadline would give newly unionized workers a guaranteed path to an enforceable contract. Some employers would also benefit from a predictable endpoint rather than open-ended negotiations, but the main beneficiary is labor.

how_it_helps.text: Requires joint selection of a mediator within 60 days if a newly certified union and employer have not reached a first contract.
Lets the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service appoint a mediator if the two sides cannot agree on one.
Allows either the employer or the union to send remaining disputes to binding arbitration 30 days after a mediator is selected, ending the employer's ability to stall indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing a new union bear the cost: binding arbitration removes their ability to delay a first contract until workers give up, and an arbitrator could impose wage, benefit, or scheduling terms the employer would not have accepted voluntarily. Employers opposed to the bill would argue this limits flexibility in setting initial employment terms.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration puts a third party in charge of writing the terms of a first contract, which can produce agreements neither side would have chosen and reduce the employer's control over wages and staffing decisions it currently negotiates directly.
The bill only covers newly certified unions; it would not help workers whose union has been negotiating a first contract for years or whose organizing vote predates the law.
A fixed timeline could discourage good-faith bargaining by making either side wait out the clock rather than negotiate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For newly unionized workers the benefit is concrete: a guaranteed endpoint to first contract talks instead of a process an employer can stretch out indefinitely. The cost falls on employers, who lose the leverage of delay and must accept an arbitrator's terms if talks fail. The bill is narrow, so it would not change conditions for the vast majority of workers who are not in the middle of a first contract fight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on day one of the 115th Congress, and the committee never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appear in the action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years in Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who oppose mandatory arbitration of first contract negotiations are better off, since the proposal died without ever reaching a vote. Nothing changed for newly unionized workers, who continue to negotiate first contracts under existing law with no deadline.

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die at the end of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of where members stood beyond the sponsor's support.

industries.note: The bill would have removed the option of stalling first contract negotiations indefinitely, since either side could send unresolved terms to binding arbitration after 90 days. Employers who use that leverage to avoid agreements would have lost it.
New unions would have gained a guaranteed path to an enforceable first contract, strengthening the value of winning an organizing election. This runs alongside newly unionized workers' interest.
